phonemes.desc: ma, 'mother' — the universal Andean title of sacred maternity.
The reduplicated second syllable, stressed: MA-ma, soft and sustained.
Quechua q is a uvular k; qui sounds 'kee.' The word is killa/quilla, 'moon, month.'
The palatal ll, the 'ly' sound; the Spanish chroniclers wrote it quilla.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAH-mah KEE-lyah' — the chroniclers' 'Mama Quilla'; in modern Quechua orthography Mama Killa.

pronunciation.note: Mama Quilla is single-tier Tier 2: ASCII loses nothing — the q-to-k of Quechua orthography and the palatal ll are conventions the plain spelling already implies. Her name is a plain description: 'Mother Moon.'

domains.title: Mama Quilla
domains.subtitle: Moon
domains.lead: Mama Quilla — Mother Moon — is the Inca goddess of the moon, sister and wife of the Sun, mother of the dynasty's founders, and keeper of the calendar. Silver was her metal, the night her realm, and the Coya — the queen — her living image on earth.

cards.name: Mother Moon
cards.desc: The moon as mother — her name itself, and her office over fertility, women, and the night.

cards.name: Keeper of Time
cards.desc: She governed the lunar months and festival calendar — the waxing and waning that set the empire's rhythm.

cards.name: Sister-Wife of the Sun
cards.desc: Wed to Inti, her brother — the paired lights of sky, with gold for him and silver for her.

cards.name: Mother of the Founders
cards.desc: From her and Inti came Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, sent to found Cuzco and the Inca line.

symbols.name: Silver
symbols.meaning: Her metal — her shrine in the Coricancha was sheathed in silver facing the Sun's gold

symbols.name: The Crescent (Killa)
symbols.meaning: The waxing moon, the favorable phase — the very word quilla means both 'moon' and 'month'

symbols.name: The Lunar Calendar
symbols.meaning: Her arithmetic: the twelve (or thirteen) lunar months that timed festivals, planting, and war

symbols.name: The Mirror of the Coya
symbols.meaning: The queen, her earthly counterpart, who bore the moon's title and diadem

symbols.name: The Eclipse
symbols.meaning: The jaguar's attack on the moon — the omen that emptied plazas and filled the night with noise

mythology.lead: Mama Quilla's mythology comes through the colonial chroniclers — Cobo above all — who recorded a functioning state theology: the moon as mother, wife, and calendar. The tradition offers genealogy rather than epic, and it is richest where the moon meets the people — in the founding legend, the eclipse rites, and the silver shrine.

myths.title: Sister-Wife of the Sun
myths.text: The chroniclers — Cobo (Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Book 13) most fully, Polo de Ondegardo and Murúa in agreement — make Mama Quilla the sister and wife of Inti, the Sun. The pairing is cosmic administration: two lights of opposite temper and opposite metal, gold and silver, day-side and night-side, ruling the sky as the emperor and Coya ruled the earth. The Coya embodied the correspondence on earth: her title, her silver ornaments, and her seat beside the emperor all repeated the sky's arrangement at court scale, as the chroniclers noted with visible discomfort. The sibling-marriage, startling to Europeans,The sibling-marriage, startling to Europeans, marked the gods as the model of the dynasty's own endogamy — the Inca married his sister the Coya as Inti married the Moon. The theology reads like a constitution written in sky: what is highest in heaven licenses what is highest on earth.

myths.title: Mother of Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo
myths.text: From the union of Sun and Moon came Manco Cápac and his sister-wife Mama Ocllo, who were sent from the cave of origin to find the place where a golden staff would sink into the ground — the valley of Cuzco (Cobo, Book 13; the parallel accounts of Murúa and the Sarmiento de Gamboa tradition). There they taught the people to plant, weave, and worship, and there the Inca dynasty began. Later empire converted the genealogy into policy: marriages among kin kept the founding blood undiluted, so the moon's marriage quietly licensed the palace's. Mama Quilla is thus not a background figureMama Quilla is thus not a background figure but the dynasty's own mother: every emperor's claim ran through her, and the Coya her daughters-in-line embodied her office. The myth is political at its root — a capital city justified as a family homestead of the moon.

myths.title: When the Jaguar Attacks the Moon
myths.text: When the moon darkened, the Inca believed a jaguar (otorongo) was seizing her — and the whole city responded. Cobo describes the rite: a great noise of shouting, drums, and trumpets, dogs loosed and beaten toward the sky, weapons brandished, all to frighten the beast away; pregnant women hid, fearing the eclipse's shadow would mark their unborn children. The same vigilance watched the sun's darkening, rarer and grander; court astronomers observed both lights nightly, their whole science bent toward early warning. Murúa ties such omensMurúa ties such omens to the empire's anxieties, and chroniclers report an eclipse among the portents before Huayna Capac's death. The rite is theology in action: the sky is alive with predators, and the people's noise is their part of the hunt — cosmic defense as civic duty, performed by an entire city at the top of its lungs.

myths.title: The Moon's House in the Coricancha
myths.text: In the Coricancha, the golden temple of Cuzco, Mama Quilla's chamber faced the Sun's — walls sheathed in silver, her image of silver with a disc like the full moon, served by the consecrated women (mamakuna) and girls (ñustakuna) whose order she patronized (Cobo, Book 13; Polo). Cobo says her image showed a woman with a great silver disc at her breast — the full moon worn like a heart — and that white maize and shellfish were laid before her. There her calendar was kept:There her calendar was kept: the priests of the moon tracked her phases to time the festivals — among them the great moon-festival (Coya Raymi, in the month of her honor) that closed the planting season. The shrine made the theology tactile: silver for the night goddess set against gold for the day god, the two metals dividing the temple as the two lights divide the sky.

lore.syncretism: Under Spanish rule, Mama Quilla's moon was quietly reassigned to the Virgin Mary — a mapping prepared by the Virgin's own lunar iconography (the woman clothed with the sun, the moon beneath her feet) and welcomed in Andean devotion, where Marian feasts absorbed the timing of the old lunar rites. The conversion was rarely clean: eclipse rituals survived under the surface, and the moon-festival season persists in the festival calendar of Cuzco's Corpus Christi. In the twentieth century the process reversed — the indigenous movement reclaimed the moon for Mama Quilla, and modern Killa Raymi celebrations in Ecuador and Peru explicitly restore the goddess to her festival, pairing her again with Inti in the revived Inti Raymi pageants. Andean religion here shows its characteristic resilience: the moon changed name for four centuries without changing office.
lore.culturalLegacy: Mama Quilla's most durable legacy is lexical: killa/quilla, 'moon,' is also the Quechua word for 'month' — her cycles are still how millions count time, and the lunar-timed agricultural calendar remains the skeleton of Andean ritual life. Her festival, Killa Raymi or Coya Raymi (the 'moon festival,' associated with women and with September in the modern revival), is celebrated again in Ecuador and Peru as a festival of femininity and planting. The silver moon survives in the crafts: Quechua and Aymara artisans still make the crescent-disc pendants that descend from her shrine imagery. And in Cuzco's living calendar — Inti Raymi on the June solstice, with the Coya at the Sun's side — the sister-wife of the Sun remains the model of the queen: her title passed into the Spanish viceroyalty's own court etiquette.
lore.extendedMeditation: Mama Quilla embodies the Andean genius for pairing. The Inca universe is built of twinned powers — sun and moon, gold and silver, hanan and hurin, emperor and Coya — and she is the night half of the founding pair. Where the sun commands, the moon counts: her office is time, the patient arithmetic of waxing and waning by which planting, festival, and warfare were scheduled. That the dynasty's mother is the moon rather than the sun is a quiet but profound statement: empire's light may blaze, but its continuity — months, gestations, harvests — is feminine and lunar. Her eclipse myth sharpens the point: the moon's darkness is the moment the whole community must shout. A civilization, the goddess suggests, is measured not by its triumphs but by whether it makes noise for its mother when she is attacked.
lore.archaeology: The physical center of her cult was the Coricancha in Cuzco, whose curved western wall still stands beneath the Santo Domingo convent; excavations and the chroniclers' descriptions fix the moon chapel opposite the sun's — silver-clad, with her silver image facing the Punchao (the sun's golden boy-idol). The Spanish melted her silver into bullion, but the temple's plan survives in the foundations. Beyond Cuzco, moon imagery — crescents and full-moon discs — appears on colonial-era qirus (ritual cups) and in textiles that kept pre-conquest canons. Eclipse and moon observations are embedded in the architecture of state ritual sites such as the Coricancha itself, aligned to both solar and lunar standstills as modern archaeoastronomy (e.g., work associated with Dearborn and others at Cuzco) has argued.
